title: AI Literacy, Safety Awareness, and STEM Career Aspirations of Australian Secondary Students: Evaluating the Impact of Workshop Interventions
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether a one-day workshop-based AI literacy intervention changes Australian secondary students’ knowledge, confidence, ethical understanding, and STEM career aspirations. The study is motivated by concerns about adolescents’ exposure to synthetic media such as deepfakes and the need for schools to provide more explicit AI literacy rather than leaving learning to incidental exposure.

The intervention was the Day of AI Australia workshop sequence, delivered in three New South Wales government high schools to Years 7–10 students. The program covered AI foundations, ethics, safety and privacy, misinformation/deepfakes, and AI in careers. Data came from anonymous pre- and post-surveys, with quantitative analysis of changes in AI knowledge, AI recognition in everyday tools, and career interest, plus thematic analysis of open-ended reflections.

Results showed that students reported significantly higher AI knowledge and confidence after the workshops, and they became better at identifying AI in platforms such as Netflix, Spotify, TikTok, and Face Unlock. Students also showed increased interest in AI, computer science, and engineering careers, though these effects were small. The authors conclude that short AI literacy workshops can produce immediate gains in conceptual understanding and awareness, but sustained and longitudinal instruction is likely needed to influence longer-term aspirations and durability of learning.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: General generative AI tools and chatbot-like systems used for text, image, and other content generation, without a single named product focus.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper discusses students’ use of general generative productivity tools and AI chatbots as part of baseline AI exposure and literacy (e.g., ChatGPT, Canva Magic Write/Design, Google Gemini), but the intervention itself is a workshop-based AI literacy curriculum rather than a study of a single generative AI product.

findings.finding_summary: Students reported higher self-reported AI knowledge after the workshop intervention, with the largest effect size for "Knowledge about AI" (p < .001, r = .445; pre n=200, post n=158). This is a mixed-methods pre/post comparison using separate samples rather than paired individuals.

Students also showed improved understanding of how AI systems are trained and how AI bias/errors work, with medium effect sizes. The paper reports "Understand AI training" (p < .001, r = .399; pre n=201, post n=160) and "Understand AI bias/errors" (p < .001, r = .302; pre n=200, post n=160).
findings.measure: Understanding of AI training and AI bias/errors
findings.sample_size: pre n=201/post n=160; pre n=200/post n=160

findings.finding_summary: Recognition of AI in everyday tools increased for some platforms after the workshop, including Spotify (+16.2%), TikTok (+12.8%), Netflix (+27.1%), and Face Unlock (+11.2%). The paper interprets this as students better recognizing AI within algorithmic recommendation systems rather than only in overt chatbots.
findings.measure: Proportion identifying tools as using AI
findings.effect_size: percentage-point change: Spotify +16.2, TikTok +12.8, Netflix +27.1, Face Unlock +11.2
findings.confidence_interval: reported for proportion differences in table, but not summarized as a single CI
findings.sample_size: N=368 total responses (pre n=205 + post n=163)

findings.finding_summary: Interest in AI-related careers increased significantly after the workshops, but the reported effect sizes were small. The paper reports increased interest in AI (p < .001, r = .189; pre n=175, post n=157), Computer Science (p = .005, r = .115; pre n=176, post n=157), and Engineering (p = .029, r = .119; pre n=178, post n=157).
findings.measure: STEM career interest (AI, Computer Science, Engineering)

quality_tier_rationale: This is a mixed-methods pre/post workshop study with separate pre and post samples rather than paired student-level data, so it is observational/QED-like rather than a randomized trial. The evidence is useful but has notable design limitations and no subgroup moderator analysis.
impact_tier_rationale: Several literacy-related outcomes show medium effects, including AI knowledge (r = .445) and understanding AI training (r = .399), which meet the medium-impact threshold. Although some outcomes are small, the main literacy gains are substantial enough to place the study in blue for impact.
